original_summary: The public goods game: each of n players privately splits an endowment between keeping it and a shared pot, which is multiplied by a factor below 1 per player and shared equally, so keeping is individually best and contributing is socially best. The previous adaptation, Guarded Commons, was a 4-player, 10-round version with Contribute, Sanction or Keep, simultaneous talk, and a 190-point target where exactly one reacher wins.

review.evidence: In the original, keeping strictly dominates contributing. In Guarded Commons, SANCTION paid 5m - 3 + 8k, which is never below 17 per round and grows with every keeper. Against random play, always-S won 92% of games and lost 0%. Against any opponents it could not do worse than 17 per round, and keepers were ruined by it. One simple policy controlled the game.

There is no luck, but the transfer from keepers to sanctioners was so large that the skilful questions (when to trust, when to punish, whom to suspect) were replaced by 'always sanction'. A careful cooperator could not out-score a mechanical sanctioner.
Once 'always sanction' is found, nothing remains to improve. The original one-shot game is solved at contribute 0.

Choices are hidden and only counts are announced, which is good material for inference. But a sanctioner profits whether or not anyone kept, so there was no reason to infer who was defecting or to coordinate punishment.
All scores and the target check are plain arithmetic on the counts of each action.
The game uses simultaneous polls, counts, fixed rounds and simultaneous talk. It needs no board and about 10 steps per round.

problems: P1: SANCTION paid a profit of 8 per keeper and at least 17 per round in every case, so always-S could not lose and won 92% against random play.
P2: Because sanctioning was profitable on its own, punishment needed no coordination and no inference about who kept. Talk and the anonymous count announcements did little work.
P3: Sanctioning when nobody kept cost only 3 against a target that allowed it, so permanent sanctioning was a safe default rather than a costly bet.

P4: In the original game, keeping dominates contributing, and under a highest-total rule a keeper always gains relative to contributors. A plain public goods game therefore has a policy that cannot lose.

changes.what: A sanctioner's reward now scales with the number of OTHER sanctioners: 4 x (keepers) x (other sanctioners). A lone sanctioner earns nothing from keepers and only pays the guard cost.
changes.why: Punishment now pays only when it is coordinated. Against random play, a sanctioner averages about 14.7 per round (about 147 in total), far below the target, so always-S no longer wins.

changes.what: Sanctioning costs 3 per round. With no keepers, a sanctioner scores 17 against a contributor's 20, so a player who always sanctions in an honest group ends on 170, below the 185 target, and loses.
changes.why: Sanctioning becomes a real bet that someone is keeping. It loses when nobody is.

changes.what: The fine is 6 per sanctioner paid by each keeper. Three coordinated sanctioners facing one keeper score 20 each (200 over a game) while the keeper scores 7.
changes.why: A persistent free rider can now lose: an organised group still reaches the target and leaves the keeper as the only one short. Always-K is no longer unloseable.

changes.what: The target is lowered from 190 to 185. The rule stays: exactly one reacher wins, otherwise a draw.
changes.why: All-contribute gives 200 and reaches the target. A group that starts punishing a steady keeper as late as round 4 still reaches 185. A free rider must keep unpunished at least 4 times to push the others below 185 and win alone. Cooperation can recover after a betrayal, and a betrayal can still pay.

changes.what: Simultaneous talk and count-only announcements are kept, and the payoffs now give them a purpose.
changes.why: Players must agree when to sanction together, judge from the counts whether someone is keeping, and decide whether an accusation or a promise is genuine.

keeps: Each round a private choice between putting 10 tokens into a pot that is doubled and shared, or keeping them.
The tension between individual free-riding and group gain.
Costly punishment of free riders as an optional institution, as in public goods experiments with punishment.
Anonymous play: only aggregate counts are announced, as in iterated public goods experiments.
Four players, 10 rounds, and simultaneous non-binding talk.

recommendation.reason: The structure works. Only the sanction payoffs and the target needed rebalancing so that punishment must be coordinated and no simple policy is safe.

variation.name: Guarded Commons II
variation.summary: A 4-player, 10-round public goods game with anonymous contributions and a target of 185. Each round players may contribute, keep, or contribute and stand guard. Guards fine keepers, but a guard profits only when other guards stand with them. The one player who reaches the target alone wins. Otherwise the game is a draw.
variation.rules:
SETUP: Exactly 4 players. Each has a private total starting at 0. The game lasts exactly 10 rounds. The target is 185 points. Individual choices and totals are hidden from the other players until the game ends.

EACH ROUND:
1. Talk. Every player writes one short message at the same time, without seeing the others' messages. All four messages are then shown to everyone. Messages are not binding: players may propose, promise, accuse or lie.
2. Choice. At the same time and in secret, each player chooses one action. Each player holds 10 tokens this round.
   - CONTRIBUTE: put all 10 tokens into the public pot.
   - SANCTION: put all 10 tokens into the public pot, and also pay 3 points to stand guard.
   - KEEP: keep all 10 tokens as 10 points.
3. Scoring. Let c, s and k be the numbers of players who chose CONTRIBUTE, SANCTION and KEEP (c + s + k = 4), and let m = c + s be the number who paid into the pot.
   - Public pot: it holds 10 x m tokens. It is doubled and shared equally, so every player, whatever they chose, receives 5 x m points.
   - A CONTRIBUTE player scores 5 x m.
   - A SANCTION player scores 5 x m - 3 + 4 x k x (s - 1). A guard collects 4 points per keeper for each OTHER guard standing with them, so a lone guard collects nothing.
   - A KEEP player scores 10 + 5 x m - 6 x s. A keeper pays a fine of 6 points for each guard.
   Reference (round scores; C = contribute, S = sanction, K = keep):
   - 4C: C 20. 3C 1S: C 20, S 17. 2C 2S: C 20, S 17. 1C 3S: C 20, S 17. 4S: S 17.
   - 3C 1K: C 15, K 25. 2C 1S 1K: C 15, S 12, K 19. 1C 2S 1K: C 15, S 16, K 13. 3S 1K: S 20, K 7.
   - 2C 2K: C 10, K 20. 1C 1S 2K: C 10, S 7, K 14. 2S 2K: S 15, K 8.
   - 1C 3K: C 5, K 15. 1S 3K: S 2, K 9.
   - 4K: K 10.
   Each player adds their round score to their own total. Totals are never reset and may go down.
4. Announcement. The numbers of players who chose CONTRIBUTE, SANCTION and KEEP are announced to everyone. Each player is told privately their own round score and total. No one is told who chose what or anyone else's total.

END: After round 10, all totals and the full history of choices are revealed, and the winner is decided by the objective.
variation.objective: After round 10, a player reaches the target if their total is 185 or more. If exactly one player reaches it, that player wins. If two or more players reach it, or nobody does, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Full cooperation gives everyone 200 and a draw. A free rider who keeps 4 or more times without being punished pushes the others below 185 and wins alone. So the group must read the anonymous counts, work out whether someone is keeping, and punish. Punishment only pays when at least two players guard in the same round. A lone guard loses 3 points, and with 1 keeper and 2 contributors that keeper still scores 19. An unnecessary guard round also costs 3, and guarding in every round leaves a player on 170, below the target. Talk passes both tests. On reasoning, players propose joint guard rounds, accuse, promise and bluff. On conflict, every player wants to be the only one above 185 and wants others to bear the guard cost. A player who follows a call to guard when nobody else does pays 3 for nothing, and one who believes 'I'll cooperate' while the other keeps falls short. After a betrayal, cooperation still pays: the group can reach 185 even after several lost rounds, especially if it punishes together, as the final-round rescue against a keeper shows. Simple policies: always-C is exploited by keepers, always-K is crushed by three coordinated guards (it scores 70 while they reach 200), and always-S loses to honest contributors (170 against 200). Against random play every simple policy averages roughly 140 to 150 and almost never reaches 185.

model.payoff: 5*(n_C+n_S) if action == 'C' else ((5*(n_C+n_S) - 3 + 4*n_K*(n_S-1)) if action == 'S' else (10 + 5*(n_C+n_S) - 6*n_S))

simulation.text:
- numbers (seat 1's policy, outcome against random opponents): random: win 0% draw 99% loss 0%; always C: win 0% draw 93% loss 7%; always S: win 0% draw 100% loss 0%; always K: win 0% draw 100% loss 0%
- everyone playing 'always C' (best joint play): mean total 200.0; every player tied in 100% of games, so 0% are decided by the draw

balanced.evidence:
PAYOFFS (k = number of OTHER players who contribute; my score if I choose C or K):
- k=0: C 5 (N=1), K 10 (N=0). Gap: K +5.
- k=1: C 22 (N=2), K 15 (N=1). Gap: C +7.
- k=2: C 23 (N=3), K 20 (N=2). Gap: C +3.
- k=3: C 26 (N=4), K 25 (N=3). Gap: C +1.
In absolute points no option is strictly dominant. The grant creates a coordination structure, so the stated 'commons' dilemma only partly survives.

WINNER RULE (my standing against the best opponent this round):
- k=0: K ties everyone at 10. C is 10 behind the keepers.
- k=1: C ties the other contributor at 22, 2 ahead of the keepers. K ties two keepers at 15, 10 ahead of the contributor. Both are joint-top.
- k=2: C scores 23 against the keeper's 25 (2 behind). K scores 20 against the contributors' 22 (2 behind). Equal.
- k=3: C gives a four-way tie at 26. K gives 25 against 23, an outright lead of +2.
So for rank, KEEP is weakly dominant within a round: never worse, strictly better at k=0 and k=3.

THE FOCAL COOPERATIVE OUTCOME IS BROKEN BY THE WINNER RULE. The social optimum (all contribute, 26 each, total 260) ends in a four-way draw. A single keeper in any round gains +2 on every contributor. Choices are hidden and only N is announced, so the defector cannot be identified or punished individually. A keep in round 10 against three contributors wins the game outright with 259 against 257.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES:
- Always-KEEP vs three cooperators (always C): 25 against 23 every round, so 250 against 230. Wins every game.
- Always-KEEP vs three random players (p=0.5): keeper expects 17.5 per round; each random player expects 0.5×18 + 0.5×15 = 16.5. That is about +10 over the game, so it usually wins.
- Always-KEEP loses only if the other three coordinate to keep N=2 among themselves. They average 21.33 per round against its 20, which needs talk-based rotation they cannot verify.
- Always-CONTRIBUTE vs random: about 18 per round against random keepers' higher relative standing at k=0 and k=3. It loses often.
A thoughtless 'always keep' wins against cooperative and random play. That fails the check.

playable.evidence:
WHAT WORKS:
- Rules are complete: grant shares 12, 8 and 6 are integers, and the reference table matches the formulas (N=3: 15+8=23, keeper 25; N=4: 20+6=26).
- The game is finite at 10 rounds and decided by arithmetic.
- Complexity is within limits: 8 steps, 2 choice steps, 11 attributes, 1 hidden element, 0 draws, 10 rounds.
- Talk is simultaneous and is justified with 4 players: interests diverge over who contributes when N=2 is the best split, so proposals can cost the follower.
- No board, judge or clock is needed.

WHY IT FAILS (repeated fixed-length game decided by the highest total):
- In round 10, KEEP is weakly dominant for rank (see balanced), so the safe option wins the last round. That unravels backwards through the late rounds.
- After a betrayal (N=3 seen when 4 were promised), the betrayer leads by 2 and cannot be identified, since only N is announced.
- The only way for the others to catch up is to keep themselves. Cooperation therefore does not pay after a betrayal, and late rounds collapse to KEEP.
- One cooperative arrangement does resist deviation: a pre-agreed pair rotation (exactly 2 contribute, 210 each). It produces a guaranteed four-way draw, so cooperation's best case is 'nobody wins'.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE: there are no random draws, so chance contributes about 0% of the result. It is decided by choices only.

INFERENCE: there is something to infer. The announced N over 10 rounds, set against the stated promises, lets a player estimate who is lying, and the totals are hidden. A player can act on it: contribute when expecting exactly 1 other contributor (+7), keep when expecting 3 (+2 for rank), keep when expecting 0.

GOOD PLAY: when all play the intended good strategy (full cooperation or a fair pair rotation), the result is a symmetric draw, not a draw decided by luck. A player who reasons about the final rounds and the others' intentions (keeps at k=3 late) is clearly favoured over a naive cooperator.

The problems are balance and unravelling, not luck.

required_changes: Remove KEEP's rank advantage when others cooperate. Raise the grant to 36 (shares 18/12/9). Contributors then score N=2: 28, N=3: 27, N=4: 29, against keepers 20 and 25. Then lower the public return (e.g. pot ×1.5, so each player gets 3.75×N, or use 4×N with tokens adjusted) so that K still beats C when k=0 and the k=1 case remains a real dilemma. Re-derive the 4×2 table and the rank table and confirm neither option is weakly dominant for rank in any k.

Reveal each player's choice after every round (keep totals hidden if you want inference). Betrayals are then attributable, cooperation can be restored by targeted retaliation, and a defector can be singled out.
Add a sanction step. Each player may simultaneously pay 2 points to remove 4 points from one named player, so betrayal after round 1 can cost the betrayer.
Remove the last-round unravelling. Use one random draw at setup to fix a hidden end between rounds 8 and 12 (within the 1-draw limit, rounds at most 40), so no round is known to be final.
After the changes, re-test always-KEEP against three cooperators and against random play under the winner rule, and show it loses at least sometimes against sensible play.

balanced.evidence: Formulas checked: C = 5m, S = 5m - 3 + 4k(s-1), K = 10 + 5m - 6s. Every reference cell matches. For example, 3S1K gives S = 15-3+8 = 20 and K = 25-18 = 7; 1C2S1K gives S = 15-3+4 = 16 and K = 13; 1S3K gives S = 2 and K = 9. Totals over 10 rounds: all-C gives 200 each; all-K gives 100 each; always-S with no keepers gives 17x10 = 170, which is below 185. WINNER RULE applied: a player wins only if exactly one player reaches 185; otherwise the game is a draw. Full cooperation (200,200,200,200) is a draw. Full selfishness (100 each) is also a draw. The social optimum therefore earns exactly the same result as the selfish outcome, so cooperation has no point. Thoughtless policy ALWAYS KEEP: (a) Against three always-C players it gets 25/round = 250 while they get 150, so it WINS. (b) Against random opponents (each 1/3 C/S/K, E[m] = 2, E[s] = 1) its expected round score is 10+10-6 = 14, about 140 in total. The random players average less, so nobody reaches and the game is a DRAW. (c) Against sensible punishers playing 3S1K every round it gets 70 and they get 200 each. Three players reach, so it is a DRAW. (d) It can lose only if the other three engineer exactly one sole reacher. For example, A keeps while B and C contribute (2C2K: A 20, B/C 10) in 5 rounds, and 3S1K is played in 5 rounds. That gives A 200, the always-keeper 135, and B/C 150 each. But B and C then lose instead of drawing, so this is irrational kingmaking. Always-keep therefore wins or draws against every realistic opponent, and that fails the check. Always-S never reaches 185 unless others keep, so it can only draw or lose. Always-C wins nothing and is exploitable. A deviator who keeps in 4 of 10 rounds while the others contribute ends on 220 against 180, which is the only real route to a win. With 4 symmetric seats moving simultaneously there is no seat edge. The core flaw is the draw-lumping winner rule, not the payoff numbers.

playable.evidence: The actions, the formulas, the reference table and the private and public information are all fully specified, and the reference table is arithmetically consistent. The game is finite at 10 rounds and decided by arithmetic on kept totals. Stated complexity is 10 steps of 20 allowed, 2 choice steps of 4, 7 attributes of 20, 1 hidden element of 3, 0 random draws, and 10 rounds of 40, all within limits. No judge, board or clock is needed. The choice is a simultaneous poll. Talk is simultaneous, and it fits here because interests conflict. Each player prefers to be the sole reacher, while guarding only pays when at least 2 guards stand together, so it needs coordination that may be betrayed. Late rounds: K beats C by 10-6s, which is +4 or more when s ≤ 1 and negative when s ≥ 2. K therefore does not dominate in the last round if a credible guard pair exists, and cooperation can still pay after a betrayal.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: There are no random draws, so chance is about 0%. There is something to infer: the public counts plus a player's own choice reveal the multiset of the other choices, and hidden totals can be partly reconstructed from those counts. There is also a way to act on it, by guarding when a defection looks likely, or by defecting when opponents look naive. A good reasoner beats naive cooperators: keeping 4 times against 3 contributors gives 220 against 180, a sole reacher and a win. When everyone plays well (cooperate and punish) the result is a draw, but that draw is decided by the winner rule, not by luck. This passes only narrowly. Most competent games end in draws, so the edge from reasoning is small, and that is driven by the balance flaw above.

required_changes: Replace the winner rule. Among players whose total is at least 185, the highest total wins, with ties broken by fewest KEEP choices and then shared. If nobody reaches 185, all players LOSE rather than draw, so all-KEEP (100 each) becomes a shared loss and cooperation now beats selfishness.
Re-check always-KEEP under the new rule and confirm it now loses. Three guards playing 3S1K hold it to 70, so it never reaches 185, while each guard reaches 200 and the guards share the win.

Add a reference line showing that a lone defector facing two guards nets less than contributing. 1C2S1K gives K 13 against C 15, which already holds. State this explicitly so models see that guard pairs are a credible deterrent.
